subject: music
title: Elements Application: Tempo, Timbre & Texture
welcome_lead: Apply the next three elements — tempo, timbre and texture — to describe music in vivid detail.
meta_desc: GCSE Music Musical Elements Adventure 2: applying tempo (Italian terms), timbre and the four main textures in real listening.
final_note: You can describe a piece's pace, colour and layering with confidence.

concepts.def: Speed of the music, often in Italian or BPM.
Tone colour — what makes instruments sound different.

walkthroughs.body_html:
From slow to fast: Largo → Adagio → Andante (walking pace) → Moderato → Allegro → Vivace → Presto.

Tempo changes use accelerando (speeding up), ritardando (slowing down) and a tempo (back to original speed).

walkthroughs.h2: Why a violin doesn't sound like a flute
walkthroughs.body_html:
Timbre (pronounced 'tam-ber') is tone colour. Even at the same pitch and volume, a violin sounds different from a flute because of its harmonic content and attack.

Describe timbre with words like warm, harsh, bright, mellow, rich, thin, nasal, piercing. Examiners love specific, evocative timbre words.

Monophonic: a single line. Homophonic: melody + chords. Polyphonic: independent melodies interweaving (Bach fugue). Heterophonic: one melody played simultaneously with variations (gamelan, folk music).

Texture often changes throughout a piece — thinning into verses, thickening into choruses.
